name: Cosmetic tattooing (early 20th century)

lead: Cosmetic tattooing is the placement of pigment in the dermis to mimic makeup on the cheeks, lips, brows and eyes. In the early twentieth century it was marketed as a way to give pale faces a lasting complexion without daily cosmetics.

Wikipedia credits British tattoo artist Sutherland MacDonald, working in London in 1902, with perfecting a method of giving a lasting complexion to pale cheeks, and George Burchett, writing in the 1930s, with developing the technique further. The modern descendants are permanent makeup, microblading and medical tattooing.

paras: Historically, a tattooist or salon implanted tinted pigment in the skin of the cheeks, lips or brows so colour stayed after washing. Burchett wrote that salons tattooed many women, sometimes marketing it as a complexion treatment. Today the same principle is used for brows, eyeliner, lips and for camouflage such as areola restoration.

Reviews list infections, healing problems, fading and colour shift, pigment migration ('blowout'), granulomas including in sarcoidosis, allergic reactions in lip tattoos, scarring after microblading, and burning sensations in tattoos during MRI. Removal is difficult.

Lasting blush, lip or brow definition
angle.text: The tattoo itself is the cosmetic effect: coloured dermal pigment that reads as blush, lip colour or brow shape. The result is long-lasting and difficult to remove.

lead: Cosmetic tattooing places pigment in the dermis to imitate makeup on the brows, eyeliner, lips and eyelids. Early forms date to the turn of the twentieth century: in 1902 the British tattoo artist Sutherland MacDonald, at his London parlor, perfected a method of giving a lasting complexion to pale cheeks [1].

George Burchett was a major developer of the technique in the 1930s. In his memoirs he wrote that beauty salons tattooed many women without their knowledge, marketing the treatment as a complexion service [1]. Dermatological history describes tattooing for medical purposes as possibly more than 5,300 years old, with most advances in the last 100 years as instruments became quicker, cleaner and less painful [2].

The appeal was an always-on made-up look: colour on the cheeks, lips and brows that does not wipe off. Use grew in the 1970s and 1980s for restoring hair and pigment lost to disease, and is now routine [1]. The medical literature also documents a range of complications [3].

paras: MacDonald's 1902 work in London targeted pale cheeks [1]. Burchett's memoirs describe widespread salon tattooing marketed as a complexion treatment [1]. A review of tattoo history notes that interest in cosmetic and medical tattoos has concentrated in the last century, with growth in the last 50 years alongside social media [2].

In the 1970s and 1980s use grew for restoring hair and pigment lost to disease, now routine, including areola restoration, scar and vitiligo camouflage and scalp tattooing [1]. Training varies by US state, with apprenticeships averaging about nine months [1]. The FDA regulates tattoo inks as cosmetics, with loose oversight; some pigments are industrial-grade and not approved for skin contact [1].

A 2022 review lists early complications such as infections (notably herpes simplex), healing issues and aesthetic mistakes with regret, and late complications such as fading, colour shift, pigment escape, papules, nodules, granulomas associated with sarcoidosis, allergic lip reactions, eye irritation and scarring after microblading, plus burning in tattoos during MRI [3]. Eyeliner tattooing carries special risk to the meibomian glands [3].

Case reports describe sarcoidosis developing in cosmetic tattoos [4], and a periocular tattoo review reports bleeding, infection, allergy and granulomas, with visual impairment the most serious risk [5].
No studies found on early twentieth-century practice. Modern literature consists of reviews and case reports on complications and history [2][3][4][5].
